PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World

Qiang Wang∗1   Jianxin Bi∗1,3‡   Shulong Jiang∗1   Ruiyang Si1   Wenbo Huang1   Kaiqi Chen1   Jiaxin Li1   Liyun Li2   Xuanyi Li2†  Daquan Zhou1† Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

1 Introduction

Large language models can translate task instructions into robot programs that combine perception, spatial reasoning, and feedback control [11, 6]. Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra extend this interaction by executing code, inspecting observations, and adapting subsequent actions through execution feedback [16]. These capabilities make code a practical interface between high-level reasoning and physical behavior. They also raise a question beyond completing an individual task: How can coding agents turn physical interaction experience into robot capabilities that persist and improve across successive attempts?

Experience-based adaptation and iterative code modification offer ways to improve agents while keeping foundation model parameters fixed [15, 24]. In robotics, recent work has explored skill and agent-harness evolution in simulation [18], simulation-based practice followed by physical deployment [20], and policy improvement through direct robot interaction [22, 19]. Building on these developments, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) as a process in which execution experience informs code revisions and is retained as memory and reusable skills for subsequent exploration. Our focus is an empirical account of this process in real-world manipulation, tracing how capabilities are acquired, refined beyond first success, and converted into programs for deployment.

Physical exploration presents challenges at several levels. Agents must decide which experiments to run, which implementation details to revise, and when to reconsider the underlying approach. Repeated local changes may leave an unsuitable perception or control strategy intact. Execution feedback is also ambiguous: an apparent task failure can originate in motion, perception, or the procedure used to verify success. Moreover, success under one configuration does not establish robustness to changes in object positions, orientations, or task requirements. Retaining a successful implementation therefore raises further questions about its reuse on new tasks and its ability to operate without repeated online agent decisions. Understanding embodied RSI requires examining these aspects of the improvement process alongside task success.

We present PyRUA-REAL (Python-based Robot-Use Agent for Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning) as an embodied RSI framework for this study (Figure 1). A researcher agent selects experimental objectives and technical approaches, while an engineer agent implements programs, executes robot trials, and diagnoses failures. Their interaction connects local code improvement with task-level reassessment. A persistent repository records environmental facts, attempted approaches, execution outcomes, and reusable implementations, allowing later experiments to build on earlier experience while model parameters remain fixed. For deployment, the resulting code can be frozen and executed without runtime language-model calls, while still responding to live observations through its perception, control, and recovery routines. This separation enables us to study both the process of developing robot capabilities and the behavior of the programs that retain them.

Our experiments cover eight manipulation tasks on a dual-arm Franka platform, spanning reasoning, long-horizon execution, precise contact, deformable objects, and bimanual coordination. Recorded development success averages 91.1% across tasks. These rates aggregate attempts across code revisions; frozen-program performance is evaluated separately. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks yields 84.82% success, averaged equally over five capability groups, compared with reported results of 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and 22.48% for GPT-6-Astra. Our main contributions can be summarized as:

  • •

    An empirical study of skill acquisition and continued improvement through real-world interaction. Across eight physical manipulation tasks, we trace how coding agents turn exploration experience into executable robot skills and improve them beyond first successful rollout, documenting gains and trade-offs in task completion, execution time, and placement precision across program revisions.

  • •

    Case studies on the factors shaping embodied RSI. Through comparative experiments and diagnostic case studies, we examine how agent coordination, execution feedback, explicit task requirements, and previously acquired skills affect revision efficiency, robustness, and transfer to new tasks.

  • •

    An evaluation of the resulting robot capabilities and their deployment costs. Real-world evaluations compare frozen programs with online agent execution, quantifying execution-time benefits and identifying situations that still require online assistance. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks measures performance across five capability groups against reported baselines.

2 Related Work

Our work lies at the intersection of programmatic robotic control and agent-driven self-improvement, aiming to enable robots to continuously improve their capabilities through real-world interaction. We review related research in LLM for robotic control, agentic RSI, and embodied RSI.

LLM for Robotic Control. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled robot control by composing perception, planning, and control primitives into executable programs [11, 6, 5]. Recent advances further explore direct agent-driven control [7, 27, 14], as well as code-based approaches that improve action abstraction, execution feedback, and runtime efficiency [2, 16, 1]. Complementary approaches integrate programmatic skill representations with learned world and action models [12]. Agents can also propose structural priors that shape skill policy training and inform skill composition [8]. While online agent control offers flexible reasoning and adaptation, frequent model inference introduces computational overhead and latency. In contrast, executable programs enable efficient closed-loop control without continuous LLM intervention. Building on this paradigm, we employ coding agents to construct and progressively refine both reusable robot primitives and task-specific policies, while delegating high-frequency control to independently executable robot programs.

Agentic RSI. Recent research has explored improving LLM-based agents through accumulated experience and autonomous modification, without necessarily updating model parameters. Experience-driven approaches retain reflections, interaction histories, and reusable knowledge to improve subsequent decisions [15, 28]. Beyond memory-based adaptation, agentic RSI methods optimize the agents’ underlying scaffolds, execution logic, and search procedures through iterative code modification and evaluation [24, 4, 23, 26]. These approaches demonstrate how improvements can persist beyond individual attempts and benefit future problem-solving. Inspired by these developments, our work extends agentic self-improvement to physical interaction, where coding agents continuously accumulate execution-grounded knowledge and reusable control capabilities to improve subsequent robot policy generation and refinement.

Embodied Recursive Self-Improvement. Recent embodied RSI research leverages environmental feedback to autonomously improve robot policies, reusable skills, and agent capabilities. Simulation-centered approaches evolve skills and agent harnesses in virtual environments, sometimes followed by real-world transfer [18, 20, 17]. Other works investigate autonomous policy improvement through direct physical experimentation [22, 19], as well as reusable program libraries, hierarchical skill refinement, and persistent experience accumulation [13, 21, 3, 10]. Building on these advances, our work emphasizes the complete process of exploration, improvement, and deployment in the real world, rather than treating physical robots merely as a final validation platform.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

We study how executable robot policies improve through environment interaction while foundation model parameters remain fixed. Improvements persist as reusable skills and experience. We examine within-task policy improvement and cross-task experience reuse in terms of policy acquisition cost, final performance, and execution cost. The accumulated ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℳ\mathcal{M} can support reuse across tasks.

3.2 System Overview

PyRUA-REAL consists of three components: improvement, execution, and experience, as illustrated in Figure 2. The system receives a human-provided task goal (goal) and a task specification (survey), which describes the required coverage of objects, positions, orientations, and task variants. With the underlying agent model parameters held fixed, the system develops task programs through code generation, testing, and feedback analysis. The resulting task program runs independently of the development agents.

The improvement component comprises two agents with complementary responsibilities. The researcher manages the overall technical approach and specifies the objective, stopping criteria, and relevant experience for each experiment. The engineer implements these requirements, diagnoses problems through environmental interaction, and revises the code. They coordinate through structured experiment specifications and report artifacts, connecting task-level experimental decisions with implementation-level exploration.

The execution component independently runs the task program, whose perception, planning, and control components use live observations to generate actions and advance the task. The program may invoke locally deployed pretrained models, such as SigLIP [25] and SAM[9], as perception components. Execution frames, states, and logs support subsequent program revisions. The researcher organizes the resulting environmental facts, problem-solving records, and reusable implementations in the experience repository for future experiments and tasks.

3.3 Coding Agents Collaboration

The researcher and engineer address problems at different levels of granularity. The researcher considers the complete task and its required variations to choose a technical approach and decide when to change methods or advance to the next stage. The engineer focuses on implementation, environment interaction, and local diagnosis within the current experiment. Their basic unit of coordination is an experiment: a goal-directed exploration process that may include multiple code revisions and tests.

Each experiment specifies an objective, stopping criteria, and selected experience. The researcher defines the objective for the current stage, provides relevant facts, historical approaches, and skill references, and autonomously sets the stopping criteria. Besides goal completion, stopping conditions may include a rejected hypothesis, a bottleneck requiring a different technical approach, or repeated revisions without progress. When a stopping condition is met, the engineer hands the problem back to the Researcher for reassessment.

Within an experiment, the engineer may revise code and conduct multiple focused tests without executing the complete task each time. For example, when object recognition is unreliable at a particular step, the engineer can compare recognition methods at that stage. The engineer independently decides how to implement and validate these changes within the scope of the experiment.

At the end of the experiment, the engineer returns a report containing the outcome and termination reason (results), findings from the exploration (learned), supporting execution records (evidence), and the final implementation (code). The researcher uses this report to decide whether to refine the current approach, change direction, or advance to another task stage and defines the next experiment accordingly.

3.4 Persistent Experience and Skill Evolution

Experience is organized into three levels, connecting environmental knowledge and problem-solving records to reusable code (Table 1). Experience retrieval follows the agents’ division of responsibility. When exploration begins or the engineer reports an unresolved problem, the researcher consults facts and memory to select relevant historical tasks and skills. The engineer follows these references to inspect the code, assess its applicability, and adapt it to the current problem. Complete task implementations show how an approach is used throughout a task, while primitive functions provide smaller units for reuse. Adapted code must still be tested in the current environment.

The researcher updates the experience repository from the engineer’s reports, preserving useful findings from both successful and unsuccessful attempts and linking them to the corresponding implementations. Skill usage is recorded based on the skills adopted in each experiment’s final implementation; intermediate revisions and repeated calls do not count as additional uses. The researcher also decides which adapted implementations to retain as new skills and records their observed applicability and limitations.

4 Experiments and Empirical Findings

In this section, we investigate how coding agents turn physical interaction experience into improved, reusable robot programs. We first introduce the research question and hypotheses (Section 4.1), describe the experimental settings (Section 4.2), and report capability acquisition and continued improvement beyond first success (Section 4.3). We then examine agent coordination (Section 4.4), execution feedback (Section 4.5), and explicit task requirements (Section 4.6), followed by cross-task primitive-skill transfer (Section 4.7) and deployment efficiency (Section 4.8). Real-world development histories and diagnostic cases provide the primary empirical evidence, complemented by simulation evaluations and comparisons.

4.1 Research Question and Hypotheses

Our experiments address one overarching research question:

How should coding agents turn physical interaction experience into progressively more capable robot programs?

Specifically, we examine the following hypotheses, which the experimental results may support or challenge:

  • •

    H1: Accumulated physical experience supports sustained self-improvement. Retaining execution experience as memory and executable skills enables successive improvement cycles to build on prior discoveries and failures, improving robot capabilities beyond the first successful program. (Section 4.3)

  • •

    H2: Multi-agent coordination with specialized responsibilities improves RSI efficiency. Distributing task-level planning, implementation, and independent review across specialized agents is expected to improve the efficiency of successive exploration and revision cycles. (Section 4.4)

  • •

    H3: Rich execution feedback improves RSI efficiency. Visual records and robot-state information enable more effective failure diagnosis and program revision than outcome-only feedback. (Section 4.5)

  • •

    H4: Explicit task requirements improve the robustness of robot programs. Specifying objects, layouts, and task variants guides exploration and skill refinement toward better robustness on unseen task variations. (Section 4.6)

  • •

    H5: Developed primitive skills can positively transfer to new tasks. Agents given a primitive-skill library acquired on earlier tasks are expected to develop more successful programs for new tasks than agents without that library. (Section 4.7)

  • •

    H6: Consolidating exploration into executable programs improves deployment efficiency. Encoding task decisions in reusable programs reduces repeated online agent calls and execution time. (Section 4.8)

4.2 Robotic Platforms and Task Settings

We evaluate PyRUA-REAL on a dual-arm Franka platform across eight physical tasks, complemented by RoboDojo simulation tasks. Figure 3 shows the physical task scenes, and Figure 4 summarizes the selected properties of the physical tasks.

Real-world robot platform.

The system comprises two Franka Research 3 arms with Robotiq-85 grippers, a head-mounted ZED Mini camera, and wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D405 cameras. Agents receive interfaces for accessing sensor observations and issuing low-level control commands. Platform calibration results and task-specific controllers and solvers are not provided in advance; they must be established during exploration.

Real-world tasks.

We consider eight different real-world tasks illustrated in Figure 3 with evaluation focuses summarized in Figure 4: Tic-tac-toe, alternating legal piece placements on a 3×33\times 3 board; Five-block stacking, constructing a tower in a prescribed color order; Tower of Hanoi, sorting eight disks by size and placing them on a peg; Ethernet insertion, inserting an RJ45 connector into a fixed port; Towel folding, folding a towel with both arms; Push T, pushing a T-shaped object to a target pose; Block sorting, placing blocks into color-matched bins; and Block storage, collecting scattered blocks into a bowl. Detailed task configurations and completion criteria are provided in Appendix C.

Simulation tasks.

RoboDojo comprises 42 base tasks in five capability groups: Generalization, Memory, Precision manipulation, Long-horizon tasks, and Open tasks. These groups cover object and layout variations, state and sequence memory, precise alignment, multi-stage execution, and instruction grounding and reasoning, respectively. We use the full suite for capability evaluation and task subsets for studies of execution feedback and explicit task requirements; their evaluation protocols are specified with each study.

4.3 Embodied RSI Performance in the Real World and Simulated Environments

We examine whether physical interaction experience can be translated into executable robot capabilities and further improvements through embodied RSI (H1). We first report results across the eight physical tasks, then examine continued improvement beyond first successful exploration rollout and the limits of agent-free execution. Frozen-program evaluation on RoboDojo provides complementary evidence on a broader task suite.

4.3.1 Real-world capability acquisition with agent

Physical exploration produces agent-free programs for seven of the eight tasks (Figure 5). These programs execute using live perception, control, and recovery logic without runtime language-model calls. Approximate time to first success ranges from 1.5 hours for block storage to 45 hours for Push T, indicating substantial variation in acquisition cost across tasks. Ethernet insertion remains unsuccessful without online agent participation in the reported development record.

Across the seven tasks with agent-free solutions, recorded development success ranges from 91.67% to 100% (Figure 5b). These rates aggregate attempts across program revisions and describe the development record rather than the reliability of a single frozen program. Successful execution times also vary substantially across tasks (Figure 5c); their task-specific endpoints are defined in Appendix C.

4.3.2 RSI beyond the first successful rollout

The first successful execution establishes that a task is feasible, but leaves room to improve repeatability, speed, and placement precision. To examine H1, we analyze the subsequent development histories of stacking, tic-tac-toe, and Hanoi. Successive program versions show further gains, with occasional regressions and different trajectories across tasks. Figure 6 compares completion and execution time across the three tasks; Figure 7 shows stacking placement errors in position and angle. The results presented here are from exploring process and do not represent the final results of repeat tests.

Stacking improves gradually across revisions. Repeated refinement of the transfer routine improves both execution time and placement estimates. Median stack–unstack cycle time falls from 285.3 to 156.0 s, while mean visually estimated lateral error decreases from 2.69 to 0.44 mm for stacking (Figures 6 d and 7 a). Full-cycle success rises from 88.7% to 98.7% across the two reported smooth-stage evaluations; these stage-level rates are distinct from the cumulative success curve in the figure. Despite local regressions, the reductions in time and estimated error extend across multiple revisions, consistent with incremental improvements to a repeatedly executed routine. Mean absolute angular error for stacking also falls from 1.37 to 0.25∘ (Figure 7b). These errors are visual estimates, rather than independent measurements of physical accuracy.

Tic-tac-toe shows a significant change after a motion-strategy revision. Success rate rises from 50% in the first version grow to 100% in the next, with later regressions before returning to 100%. Game-and-reset time falls from 577 to 535 s overall (Figure 6 b,e). Most of this reduction occurs between V4 and V5, when time drops from 573 to 536 s. At this transition, a revision replaces sequences of elevated free-space waypoints with a single JointMotion for transfers repeated during play and reset. The two relatively stable timing ranges on either side of this revision link the observed improvement to a change in motion strategy. The success-rate regressions also show why faster execution must be checked alongside task success.

Hanoi tower shifts from improving reliability to reducing execution time. Early revisions prioritize reliable completion, with longer execution times. Median stack–unstack cycle time reaches 1402 s in the robust stage, then falls to 883 and 793 s in the two speed-focused versions (Figure 6 c,f). Full-cycle success rate fluctuates between stages, rising from 60% initially to 100% in the final version. This history illustrates a change in optimization priorities: first establish a reliable routine, then reduce its execution cost. Final version combines shorter execution with higher success rate, although intermediate revisions do not improve both together.

These histories show that embodied RSI can continue improving an executable skill after the first successful trial. Improvement can accumulate through local refinement or follow a change in motion strategy, and its direction can shift as reliability and speed become different priorities.

4.3.3 Additional Evaluation on RoboDojo

Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, PyRUA-REAL’s frozen programs achieve 84.42% capability-averaged success, compared with 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and 22.48% for GPT-6-Astra (Figure 8). The largest advantage over PyRUA-Lean is in Precision (74.00% versus 38.25%), followed by Long-Horizon (56.00% versus 43.75%), while Generalization remains slightly lower (41.17% versus 43.17%). The programs therefore perform better overall, with gains concentrated in precision manipulation and long-horizon execution. These are reported results from separate evaluations with different or unspecified seeds.

4.4 Agent Coordination for Exploration

We examine H2 through physical development histories, asking whether specialized agent responsibilities help programs improve through successive physical trials. We analyze the cost of adding a reviewer to the engineer’s revision and testing cycle, then examine cases in which local revisions continue without resolving a stalled approach.

An additional reviewer agent can slow down exploration.

We compare development records with and without a reviewer that inspects each submitted program before hardware execution. The reviewer can reject a submission but cannot modify it; the engineer must therefore revise and resubmit rejected programs. The median interval from reporting a result to starting the next physical trial is 16.9 minutes with the reviewer and 3.4 minutes without, across 40 and 9 recorded transitions, respectively (Figure 9a). Six submission–rejection–revision cycles in the Hanoi experiment take 5.1–19.0 minutes each, with a median of 8.5 minutes (Figure 9b), showing how review adds waiting before the next physical test. The reviewed phase records no verified disk-on-peg insertion over 45.0 hours, whereas the subsequent direct-testing phase reaches its first insertion 2.8 hours after the first grasp test (Figure 9c). Because the phases are sequential, the later phase may benefit from earlier exploration, so the insertion timeline does not isolate the effect of removing the reviewer. The directly observed review delays nevertheless identify a coordination cost: assigning approval to a separate agent can reduce the rate at which the system obtains new physical evidence for improvement.

Task-level reassessment can break local revision deadlocks.

Repeated local revisions can leave exploration stalled when the underlying approach remains unchanged. Figure 10 shows seven simulated and three physical task histories in which unsuccessful trials are followed by success after task-level reassessment. A single Researcher is involved throughout each history; the intervention marks its reassessment of accumulated failures and redirection of the Engineer’s exploration. In all three physical cases, the next trial succeeds, with subsequent development records totaling 3/3 successes for stacking, 1/1 for towel folding, and 3/3 for Hanoi. Progress in simulation is less uniform: Push T records 11/17 successes after reassessment, while Imitate sorting sequence records 4/11. These histories motivate bounding local revision and returning unresolved failures to the Researcher for reassessment. They associate reassessment with renewed progress, without isolating its effect from continued exploration.

4.5 RSI Based on Execution Feedback

We examine H3 by investigating how execution experience becomes actionable evidence for embodied RSI. Physical diagnostic traces connect inspected observations to program revisions and subsequent validation, while a simulation study compares feedback interfaces under a fixed revision budget.

Reliable improvement requires reliable execution feedback.

Apparent execution failures can originate in perception or verification. In tic-tac-toe, merging two touching rings causes a false placement rejection; correcting the detector makes the same image pass the unchanged acceptance criterion, without moving the robot. In stacking, successful cycles still produce large reported block-return errors. Inspection reveals an unintended camera view; correcting view selection lowers the visual error estimates, but does not independently establish more accurate motion. Embodied RSI must therefore identify whether a discrepancy comes from execution or its measurement before revising control, perception, or verification.

Richer execution feedback improves task success with reduced optimization time.

We compare three feedback interfaces on four RoboDojo tasks: basic outcome reports (B), numeric state reports (BS), and video with joint trajectories (BVJ). BS includes ground-truth object states as privileged diagnostics for revision; program execution inputs remain identical across conditions (RGB-D, calibration, and robot state). Each GPT-6-Astra Medium session generates an initial program and makes five revisions on two development layouts. Final programs are evaluated in 18 executions across six held-out layouts, with test outcomes withheld from the revising agent. Mean success is 15.3% for B, 45.8% for BS, and 54.2% for BVJ (Figure 11). Compared with B, BS increases success from 3/18 to 12/18 on Stack blocks, from 1/18 to 13/18 on Push T, and from 7/18 to 8/18 on Deposit coin. Both B and BS record 0/18 on Imitate sorting sequence, while BVJ achieves 3/18. The higher mean success with BVJ accompanies lower mean optimizer time than B: 25.4 versus 31.8 minutes for initial generation and all five revisions. Token usage is slightly higher, at 3.65 versus 3.54 million, including cached inputs. Optimizer time covers agent turns and their tools, excluding separate development and test evaluations. These results show task-dependent benefits from richer revision feedback; the BS condition additionally differs in access to privileged object-state information. Each task–condition pair has one development session, so variability across independent sessions remains unmeasured. Appendix A provides the full eight-condition protocol and cost analysis.

4.6 Towards More Robust Robot Programs

Robot programs become more robust to unseen scenarios when informed with explicit descriptions of the task variations (H4).

Agents initially develop programs under an instruction to maximize success on hidden test scenarios. We then provide numerical specifications and images defining the workspace boundaries and the ranges of target positions and orientations, and continue exploration and program revision. We evaluate both program versions on the same held-out scenarios, measuring robustness as success across these variations. Mean success increases in all five RoboDojo categories, with gains of 11.4–36.6 percentage points (Figure 12). Open tasks improve from 14.4% to 51.0%, while Memory improves from 53.8% to 65.2%. At the task level, Stack bowls improves from 0.0% to 86.4% and Fasten screws from 9.1% to 81.8%, although gains are not universal: Swap blocks declines from 68.2% to 59.1%. The results suggest that specifying the operating conditions a program must handle helps direct embodied RSI toward robustness across scenarios. This comparison includes additional exploration, so it does not isolate the effect of the added specifications alone. Appendix B provides the evaluation protocol and per-task results.

4.7 Cross-Task Experience Transfer

Previously developed primitive skills support positive transfer to new tasks(H5).

In a separate eight-task comparison, agents start new-task exploration with or without a primitive-skill library developed on earlier tasks. Programs developed with the library achieve 40.0% mean success, compared with 21.3% without it (Figure 13). Five tasks improve: classify by language and play stacking toy each gain 50 percentage points, Imitate sorting sequence gains 30, and general pickup and make toast each gain 10. fill egg holder, push T, and swap blocks show no gain. These results indicate that skills retained from previous experience can benefit subsequent tasks, with transfer benefits varying across tasks.

4.8 Offline Coding: Execution Efficiency and Capability

We distinguish two coding modes by when agent-generated code is produced relative to deployment. In offline coding (PyRUA-REAL), agents develop and revise programs through physical exploration before deployment; the resulting code is then frozen and executes without language-model calls. Its sensing, conditional actions, and recovery logic still respond to live robot observations. In deployment-time coding (PyRUA-Lean), the agent writes and executes code during the task, uses execution feedback, and generates subsequent code as needed. A code segment can perform multiple actions and local checks, but execution still includes agent calls between segments. Figure 14 compares these modes with online robot action inference without coding , which selects actions from visual observations and robot state without writing code or accessing a shell.

Converting online exploration into fixed programs avoids repeated agent decisions(H6).

In offline coding mode, the programs for tic-tac-toe, five-block stacking, and Tower of Hanoi complete execution and reset without runtime language-model calls, with median successful cycle times of 8.99, 2.99, and 16.72 minutes, respectively. On tic-tac-toe and stacking, online coding with PyRUA-Lean takes approximately 4.6–5.0 times as long as offline coding with PyRUA-REAL; online action selection with GPT-6-Astra takes approximately 9.9–11.5 times as long (Figure 14). Agent thinking accounts for 63–90% of the recorded online execution time. For stacking, PyRUA-Lean spends 10.6 of 13.7 minutes thinking; its remaining 3.1 minutes are close to the program’s 2.99-minute cycle. Thus, most of this observed timing gap comes from waiting for agent decisions. Neither online baseline completes Hanoi within 120 minutes. The comparison concerns execution time and excludes the cost of online exploration and program development.

Precise, contact-rich tasks can still require online agent assistance.

The efficiency of offline coding depends on whether the frozen program handles the conditions encountered during execution. Ethernet insertion, which requires precise connector alignment and contact with the port, exposes a limitation of the current code: the development records contain 0/4 successes with scripted execution and 10/17 with a workflow using GPT-6-Astra Medium for online decisions. This assisted workflow combines programmed motion with online assessment and decisions between stages; it does not yet provide agent-free execution in offline coding mode. In one successful run, motion takes 281.8 s and inter-stage checks and decision gaps take 220.8 s, accounting for 44% of the total 502.7 s. These gaps include visual checks and human review and therefore cannot be attributed entirely to agent thinking. The higher observed success rate supports retaining online assistance where the current program remains unreliable.

5 Discussion

Method selection can limit self-improvement.

The deadlocks in Section 4.4 suggest that progress can be limited by which methods an agent considers. Depth and calibration errors constrained geometric localization: stacking progressed with local visual alignment and contact feedback, while Hanoi combined coarse localization with wrist-camera feedback. In simulated general pickup, success improved after a human suggested SigLIP, a visual model the agent had initially overlooked. These cases indicate that the ability to implement and refine a method does not ensure that useful alternatives will be explored. A practical implication is to include explicit comparisons of alternative perception and control strategies when the current approach repeatedly fails.

Human assistance can shape the skills agents acquire.

The SigLIP case in the preceding paragraph illustrates how guidance can expand the methods considered during exploration. Human input also resolved an episode in which an agent repeatedly routed around a false contact detection. When human assistance was unavailable, the Hanoi agent developed a strategy for pushing hard-to-grasp disks into accessible positions; this strategy was later reused in tic-tac-toe. These observations suggest that intervention affects both immediate progress and the recovery skills retained for future tasks. Reports of autonomous improvement should therefore document what humans contributed and which operations the resulting program performs independently. The cases motivate studying when to intervene, without establishing an optimal level of assistance.

Offline programs may still need online agent assistance.

Successful online exploration and conversion into an executable program do not ensure that its encoded logic covers every situation encountered during evaluation. A fixed program can respond through its implemented perception, control, and recovery routines, but situations beyond those routines may still require an online agent to interpret observations and adapt the next action. The Ethernet insertion results in Section 4.8 illustrate this limitation of the current implementation: successful execution still uses online decisions between programmed motion stages. This suggests a deployment strategy that combines efficient offline execution with online assistance when the program cannot resolve an encountered situation. Determining when to invoke the agent and whether its decisions can subsequently be incorporated into reusable code remains an open question.

6 Conclusion

We investigated embodied RSI through real-world robot experiments with PyRUA-REAL, where coding agents accumulate physical experience as memory and executable skills. The real-world experiments demonstrate how physical exploration can produce progressively improved robot programs that retain acquired capabilities and execute without repeated agent decisions. This connects recursive self-improvement through physical interaction to efficient deployment, with progress assessed by the robust and independence of the resulting programs. Our findings provide an empirical basis for developing embodied RSI systems that turn physical experience into reliable robot capabilities for robustness deployment.

Appendix A Execution Feedback: Protocol, Costs, and Diagnostic Traces

Information supplied for revision.

Table 2 defines the eight conditions evaluated on all four tasks. The main-text comparison focuses on B, BS, and BVJ to contrast basic outcomes, numeric state diagnostics, and video with joint trajectories. BS includes privileged ground-truth object states supplied to the revising agent. The remaining conditions and revision histories are reported below. The persistent optimizer is GPT-6-Astra with medium reasoning effort. It receives a task description, interface specification, and a shared calibration observation before generating revision 0. Each condition uses an isolated workspace and a single retained session through revision 5; delegation is disabled. Feedback comes only from development layouts 5 and 6. Test layouts are 32–37, except that Deposit coin layout 35 is replaced by 44 for every condition after a zero-action initialization failure. Test outcomes are not supplied to the optimizer.

Execution inputs and scope.

The programs in this diagnostic study use the same RGB-D, calibration, and robot-state interface. Object-state feedback, which is part of ground truth, is additionally supplied to the optimizer in the three marked conditions.

Checkpoint and sampling protocol.

There is one independently initialized exploration session per task–condition pair. The main comparison contains 32 sessions, each with one initial generation and five revisions. Every final program is tested on six layouts with three executions per layout: 18 executions per cell and 576 in total. The fixed-revision comparison in Figure 11 uses revision 5, while Figure 16 uses the separate retrospective selection rule below. Figure 15 displays the full revision trajectories.

A.1 Observed Development Cost

Cost through the selected version.

Figure 16 uses all eight conditions; B, BS, and BVJ are labeled, while hollow diamonds mark privileged diagnostic conditions. For each task–condition pair, all revisions 0–5 are scored on the same six test layouts using the first valid execution per layout, including at revision 5. If any revision achieves at least 4/6 successes, we select the highest-scoring revision, breaking ties in favor of the earliest. Otherwise, we retain revision 5, even if an earlier revision has a higher score below 4/6. Selection uses test scores, not development scores; the selected-version scores are therefore retrospective summaries.

Costs sum recorded optimizer turns, including retries, from initial generation through the selected revision. Each plotted coordinate is the arithmetic mean over four tasks. The ordinary least-squares fit across the eight condition means has R2=0.691R^{2}=0.691.

All sessions continue through revision 5. Selected-version costs measure work accumulated through the selected revision; Table 3 reports these costs alongside the full exploration costs.

Across the eight condition means, selected-version success is associated with lower cumulative optimizer time (R2=0.691R^{2}=0.691). With video and joint trajectories, selected-version success is 58.3%, compared with 12.5% for basic outcomes; cumulative optimizer time is 19.1 versus 31.8 minutes and tokens are 2.43 versus 3.54 million. Because selection uses test outcomes, these retrospective summaries do not establish that an agent could identify the selected version or stop at it online.

Full exploration cost and measurement scope.

Full exploration costs include initial generation and all five revisions. Optimizer time is the sum of agent-turn durations, including tools invoked within those turns. Separate simulator wall time covers development evaluations, excluding queueing. Tokens are total input plus output tokens accumulated across turns, including cached input. Test evaluation costs are excluded.

A.2 Evidence Actually Inspected in Physical Tasks

A physical failure report does not by itself identify what should change. The traces below show which observations the agent inspected, the revision it made, and the check that followed. We distinguish direct image inspection from diagnosis recorded in experiment logs.

Opening a failed placement image reveals a detector error.

During tic-tac-toe setup, a red-ring transfer is rejected because its reported placement error is 80.6 mm, above the 25 mm threshold. The engineer reads execution.json and calls view_image on head-003-placed.png in the same tool invocation. The image contains five red rings, but the execution record contains only four detections: two touching rings share one contour. The mismatch directs the revision to segmentation. Figure 17 shows the actual image and an excerpt of the diff between the frozen pre- and post-fix sources. The new helper splits an outer contour only when it contains exactly two holes larger than 60 pixels in area, using the bisector of their centers.

The agent reprocesses the same image and obtains five detections; the nearest ring is now 5.7 mm from the target under the unchanged threshold. It then runs 50 regression checks, including the failure image and obstruction rejection, and checks 178 fresh static perception frames. After restarting the physical task, it reads the new execution events and confirms the initial stock transfer and the first blue and red placements. This establishes a verifier repair; the same-image comparison is not a new physical placement, and the 178 frames are not 178 manipulation trials.

Depth and gripper logs reveal why towel grasps close in the air.

A towel-unfolding trace provides a complementary change to physical execution (Figure 18). In cycle_142100, cycle 4, the left gripper exhausts six re-grasp attempts and aborts. The agent’s iteration record compares the stored table plane with the local wrist-depth fit and reconstructs pad heights from the logged arm states. Across the failed cycles, the stored plane is 25–35 mm higher than the local fit, so its descent floor can leave the pads above the cloth.

The recorded revision uses the left wrist’s local table plane when its fit has RMS error below 3 mm and at least 3,000 points. It retains the force probe (4 N rise trigger, 10 N hard limit) and expresses the descent target and re-grasp floor relative to that plane. In the next run, cycle_143600, cycle 1, the left gripper captures the towel on the first descent, with a 1.4 mm RMS fit over 6,496 points. The log reports both grippers closed and an unfolded extent of 0.30×0.420.30\times 0.42 m. This is one recorded unfold-stage recovery, not a repeated full-task success rate. The following cycle stops on a connection error. Here the evidence is the raw execution logs and the agent’s contemporaneous diagnosis; no corresponding image-open call is claimed.

Appendix B Generalization under Explicit Task Requirements: Per-Task Results

Table 4 reports the success rates underlying the category means in Figure 12. Both policies are evaluated on identical hidden layouts; layouts used to select the baseline policy are excluded. Programs receive RGB-D observations, including simulator-rendered depth.

Appendix C Physical Task Configurations and Completion Criteria

Tic-tac-toe.

The two arms alternate legal moves on a 3×33\times 3 board. The left arm places blue square-frame pieces and the right arm places red rings. A game terminates with a win or draw. The complete-cycle measurements also include clearing the board and returning the pieces to their respective sides.

Five-block stacking.

Five blocks initially lie on the table. The robot stacks the blocks to form a freestanding tower. Complete-cycle measurements include dismantling the tower in reverse order and returning the four upper blocks to their table positions.

Tower of Hanoi.

The robot sorts eight disks by size and places them onto the middle peg, from largest at the bottom to smallest at the top. This task evaluates ordered disk manipulation and repeated hole–peg alignment, rather than solving the conventional three-peg transfer puzzle. Complete-cycle measurements also include removing the disks and returning them to the table.

Ethernet insertion.

The robot grasps a yellow-booted RJ45 connector from the table and inserts it into the Ethernet port of a fixed computer chassis. Completion requires the connector to remain seated after the gripper releases it and retreats. Electrical connectivity is not evaluated.

Towel folding.

The towel initially lies flat on the table. The two arms grasp it and fold it over onto itself, requiring coordinated manipulation of a deformable object. Evaluation covers the folding operation only.

Push T.

The robot pushes a T-shaped object across the table to align its position and orientation with a target pose. Manipulation is performed through pushing, without grasping or lifting the object.

Block sorting.

The robot identifies orange and dark-blue blocks and places them into their corresponding color bins. Each trial covers sorting the specified blocks and combines visual discrimination with repeated pick-and-place operations.

Block storage.

The robot collects scattered blocks into a bowl. Success requires storing all blocks. Missed grasps followed by successful recovery remain part of the same trial.
